title: A novel called Sundri
hookLine: Vir Singh's heroine Sundri gave young Sikhs a story of courage

cards: A girl is carried off from her family by a powerful man. Her brother rides after her with a small band of Sikh fighters and brings her back. The obvious ending is a wedding, a quiet house, a safe life.
Instead, she chooses the forest. She takes amrit, joins the Khalsa, and lives with the band in the hard years when Sikhs were hunted. She cooks, nurses the wounded, rides, and refuses to be afraid.
Her name is Sundri, and she is the heroine of a novel by Bhai Vir Singh.

teach.b: First, the setting. Vir Singh set the story in the years of the jathas, the small bands of Sikhs living in forests and hills while they were hunted. Sikh memory calls those years a time of martyrs.
Sundri brought that history close, through one young woman's eyes. Second, the heroine. Sundri isn't a decoration in someone else's story.
She makes the choices. She takes amrit, receives a new name, and becomes a full member of the Khalsa. She serves in the langar and nurses the wounded.
In the novel she even tends to a wounded enemy soldier, because seva, selfless service, doesn't ask which side someone fought on. Third, why a novel. A history book can tell you what happened.

teach.h: A NOVEL LETS YOU LIVE INSIDE.
teach.b: A novel lets you live inside someone. This one invites young Sikh readers, girls and boys alike, to walk beside their ancestors in danger, with a woman at the center of the story.
For readers in the reform years, this was part of the renewal: not a lecture on faith, but a heroine to admire. Fourth, the Gurus behind it.
In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak asks why we should call woman lesser, when from her kings are born.
Readers can hear that line in Sundri's story. She lives as an equal in the Khalsa, carries its danger, and keeps its compassion.

how: Sundri is still read by Punjabi readers and in Sikh schools, and her story is retold to young Sikhs as an example of courage, service and equality in the Khalsa.

games.q: you're Sundri. your brother's band has brought you safely back. the hunted years are all around. what do you do?
o: return home and stay out of danger.
take amrit and live with the Khalsa band.
games.why: Sundri takes amrit, joins the Khalsa, and lives with the band, serving the wounded, even an enemy.

practice: Bring to mind a brave person who stayed kind, from a book, your family, the news or your own street, and picture the moment they could have run and didn't, or could have been cruel and weren't.
Stay with that moment, and notice where courage and kindness meet in it. If you pray, say Waheguru softly as you stay there.

wordCard.voice: Sundri, the heroine of Bhai Vir Singh's novel, a young woman who joins the Khalsa in the hard years, serves the wounded, and lives with courage. Today's word.

orig.note: sundri: beautiful; the heroine's name, and the novel's title.

carryVoice: Your line: a heroine for readers. Through her, a picture of what a Sikh life could look like. Until next time.
